MERA access and encoding¶

What changes when the same number of sites arrive in different combinations?¶

Two observers collect the same number of sites from the same encoding. Each receives every individual site equally often. Do they acquire the same information about the diary? The answer depends on which sites arrive together and how the encoding distributes the diary's correlations among them. Here both observers collect exactly three of eight sites.

This notebook accompanies the November 5, 2026 version of Evlondo Cooper III's From Preservation to Possession: The Physical Conditions for Black-Hole Information Recovery. It develops the paper's comparison of access patterns at fixed collection size and follows its finite-MERA methods. The encoding is a small, explicit quantum system: one logical qubit enters an eight-site binary MERA with bond dimension two, seven isometries, and six disentanglers. Its tensors are random and unoptimized. This gives us a controlled setting in which to ask what an observer's collection description determines.

We will begin with the collection geometry, follow one encoding in detail, and then examine the 64-encoding ensemble. A paired tree intervention and an independent Haar comparison help identify what each result depends on. Finally, a linear-algebra calculation makes the missing collection information explicit.

Collection geometry · One encoding · Ensemble · Intervention · Complementary access · Sufficiency · Verification

Before we calculate¶

The diary is the logical qubit whose information we track. Its reference, $Q$, is an untouched qubit initially maximally entangled with it. The encoding, $V$, distributes the diary over eight boundary sites, $B_0,\ldots,B_7$. A collection mask, $S$, identifies which sites reach the observer. The observer receives a classical record of that mask. The scores describe the information available at collection; a subsequent receiving process would transfer it into retained memory.

The default mode, saved, reads the supplied ensemble results and tensors, then executes the worked example, reaggregation, bootstrap analysis, 66 causal-cone contraction checks, and exact-null controls. The alternative, regenerate, generates the full ensemble in a fresh process, compares it with the reference results, and analyzes the new outputs. Both modes use the same numerical settings.

To regenerate, change MODE, choose a new RUN_NAME, and restart the kernel and run all cells. The study-process budget is 30 minutes and 2 GiB, checked between completed seeds. Setup and command-line instructions are in the MERA README.

Displayed ensemble: supplied study results. Worked-example and statistical checks execute below.

Collection geometry: equal size, equal individual access¶

One observer samples uniformly from the eight cyclic windows of three adjacent sites. The other samples uniformly from all $\binom83=56$ triples. The ring makes adjacency periodic: $\{7,0,1\}$ is a contiguous window. A particular noncontiguous mask such as $\{0,3,6\}$ illustrates a choice available to the uniform protocol.

Every choice contains three sites. In the contiguous protocol, each site appears in three of the eight windows. In the uniform protocol, it appears in $\binom72=21$ of the 56 triples. Both inclusion probabilities are therefore $3/8$. We can verify this directly before examining any quantum information.

Figure 1. Both highlighted masks contain three sites. Adjacency changes which sites are collected together; averaging over each complete protocol gives the same inclusion probability at every site. The uniform protocol also includes the eight contiguous masks.

The equalities above describe the detector's individual efficiencies and collection size. They do not yet tell us how diary correlations are distributed among the combinations of sites. We will compare the information made available by those combinations.

A first look at the result. Each point is one encoding's contiguous-minus-uniform information gap. White diamonds mark means and dark segments show approximate 95% bootstrap intervals for those means. All 64 MERA gaps are positive. The following calculations explain the score, reproduce its values, and establish what the paired and independent comparisons can tell us.

The encoding behind the comparison¶

An isometry preserves the logical inner products while expanding one input into two outputs. Here each $w$ is a $4\times2$ matrix satisfying $w^\dagger w=I_2$. Seven such tensors expand the diary from one site to two, four, and eight. A disentangler $u$ is a $4\times4$ unitary acting on two sites between expansions or at the boundary. In this encoding direction, it redistributes correlations before collection.

The diagram below is drawn from the ordered graph in audited_architecture.json. In particular, it includes the ordered periodic gates $(3,0)$ and $(7,0)$. The first listed site is the first tensor leg. Boundary site 0 is the most significant bit in the dense basis. No disentangler follows the first expansion to two sites.

Figure 2. The actual finite binary MERA. Each split periodic gate has two end blocks bearing the same tensor name; they are the two legs of one gate. The edge table resolves all ordered inputs and outputs. Isometry legs are (left output, right output, input); unitary legs are (first output, second output, first input, second input).

This finite network retains an open logical input at its top, so it defines a two-dimensional encoded subspace rather than a single optimized state. Its binary expansion and intermediate disentanglers follow the architecture described by Evenbly and Vidal, Algorithms for entanglement renormalization (2009). The next section evaluates local operators through this graph and compares them with full-matrix calculations.

Each paired tree keeps all seven isometries of its MERA partner. The Haar comparison changes both locality and tensor structure, and its samples are independent of the MERA/tree pairs.

Check the local calculation and three exact nulls¶

Can a local boundary observable be evaluated without carrying the whole encoding through the calculation? Starting at its boundary support, move backward through the ordered graph. An untouched isometry or unitary cancels with its adjoint. A touched tensor is contracted only with the current operator and the identity legs it needs. Support is determined by connectivity, even when coefficients vanish. In the tree, exact identity gates simply relabel wires.

The following calculation loads the frozen exploratory MERA/tree pair, seed 20260918, and verifies its tensor hashes. This pair is separate from the 64-pair ensemble. An independently specified graph fixes the ordered legs, including the periodic gates. For each encoder, ascend $X_i,Y_i,Z_i$ at all eight sites, the eight nearest-neighbor $Z_iZ_{i+1}$ operators, and $X_7Y_0$. Compare each complete logical $2\times2$ operator with full-matrix evaluation through all three encoding implementations. That gives 33 observables per encoder, giving 66 causal-cone contraction checks. The trace below shows the periodic example's retained and canceled tensors.

Three controls ask why an access gap should disappear:

  • Remove reference correlation. Apply the logical depolarizing channel before encoding. The boundary marginal is unchanged, while its reference correlation vanishes. Evaluate all 256 boundary subsets for each encoder.
  • Balance complementary access. For the pure Bell-encoded state, complementary four-site scores sum to one. Both the eight cyclic windows and all 70 four-site subsets are complement-balanced, so their means are one half.
  • Remove preferred boundary labels. Enumerate all $8!=40,320$ permutations and relabel each cyclic triple. Each triple occurs exactly 5,760 times among the $8!\times8$ choices, so the permutation-averaged cyclic score equals the uniform-subset score. The subset identity remains a readable flag; no unlabeled state mixture is substituted.

All checks use the $10^{-10}$ tolerance. Raw eigenvalues, complete logical operators, support traces, and permutation results are saved in verification/finite_checks/. These tests concern an unoptimized finite encoding, not a physical ground state or an Ising benchmark.

Follow the diary through one encoding¶

Prepare the diary $A$ and reference $Q$ in the Bell state $|\Phi^+\rangle_{QA}=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Only the diary enters the encoding. The joint state is

$$|\Psi\rangle_{QB}=(I_Q\otimes V)|\Phi^+\rangle_{QA}.$$

The reference lets us track correlations belonging to the original diary. For a collected subset $S$, trace out the uncollected boundary sites to obtain $\rho_{QB_S}$. Its mutual information is

$$I(Q:B_S)=S(Q)+S(B_S)-S(QB_S),\qquad e(S)=\frac{I(Q:B_S)}{2S(Q)}.$$

Here $S(\rho)=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log_2\rho)$ is von Neumann entropy in bits, and $S(Q)=1$ bit. Mutual information ranges from zero to two bits for this reference. Thus $e(S)$ ranges from zero to one: zero means the collected state has no reference correlation, and one means it carries the full two-bit mutual information. This access score describes the supply offered to a receiver. A recovery-fidelity calculation asks a different question about what a decoder can reconstruct.

We load the saved tensors for seed 101001, the first encoding in the ensemble. Their file and array hashes are checked before use. The helper calls the unchanged contraction and dense routines, compares their encodings, and evaluates every three-site reduction. It also confirms that this seed's paired tree retains all seven isometries.

Figure 3. All 56 subset scores for the first MERA seed in the ensemble. Squares identify the eight cyclic windows. The horizontal lines are the two protocol means. The complete table preserves subset identities so every point can be traced to a collection mask.

These means describe channels whose classical subset flags remain available. Write $F$ for that flag. Because the input-independent choice contributes no reference information by itself, the chain rule gives

$$I(Q:FB_S)=I(Q:F)+I(Q:B_S\mid F)=\sum_S w(S)I(Q:B_S).$$

Consequently, $e_C=\frac18\sum_{S\in\mathcal C_3}e(S)$ and $e_U=\frac1{56}\sum_{|S|=3}e(S)$ are the operational scores of the flagged protocols. Averaging density matrices after discarding the mask would describe a different channel. The difference $\Delta=e_C-e_U$ asks which protocol supplies more reference information for this encoding.

The positive gap is already a fixed-size witness: equal individual efficiencies leave the answer undetermined. We next ask how this behavior varies across the full ensemble.

From one encoding to the ensemble¶

The study contains 64 independent MERA draws with seeds 101001 through 101064, their paired trees, and 64 independent Haar isometries with seeds 202001 through 202064. The original exploratory seed, 20260918, remains a separate regression check and contributes to none of these estimates.

Each encoding contributes one contiguous mean, one uniform mean, and their gap. We recompute these from all 10,752 saved subset rows using accurate summation, then compare them with the reference encoding and pair tables. The 56 overlapping subsets of an encoding are components of its score, not independent statistical replicates.

For uncertainty over the random-encoding distributions used here, the study uses 20,000 encoding-level bootstrap resamples. The MERA/tree pair indices are drawn together, followed by a separate independent Haar index array, from PCG64 seed 303001. Approximate 95% intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of resampled means, with linear interpolation. Equal list positions do not create a pairing between Haar and structured samples.

What do the disentanglers change?¶

For each MERA draw, replace its six disentanglers with identities while preserving its seven isometries, Bell reference, tensor connectivity, and collection channels. The resulting encoder is a tree tensor network. This paired intervention measures the effect of the disentanglers while keeping the same seven isometries.

Define the paired gap change as

$$\Gamma=\Delta_{\mathrm{MERA}}-\Delta_{\mathrm{tree}}.$$

Positive $\Gamma$ means the MERA encoding has a larger signed contiguous-minus-uniform gap than its paired tree; negative $\Gamma$ means it has a smaller signed gap. We display both gaps and every paired effect so the mean cannot conceal attenuation or an ordering reversal.

The same encoding, complementary access¶

The joint reference–boundary state is pure. If $S^c$ is the complement of a collected subset, purity gives $S(QB_S)=S(B_{S^c})$ and $S(QB_{S^c})=S(B_S)$. Adding the two mutual informations cancels the boundary entropies:

$$I(Q:B_S)+I(Q:B_{S^c})=2S(Q),\qquad e(S)+e(S^c)=1.$$

Complementing the eight cyclic triples gives exactly the eight cyclic five-site windows. Complementing all 56 triples gives all 56 five-site subsets. Each five-site protocol mean is therefore one minus its three-site counterpart, so

$$\Delta_5=-\Delta_3.$$

This reversal uses the same states. It is an exact consequence of purity, not another independent statistical finding. The saved five-site reductions were calculated directly by both partial-trace paths. We check them against the identity rather than using the identity to manufacture the comparison.

Maximum direct-five-site mean disagreement: 4.685e-14

Figure 7. Squares show three-site gaps; circles show their complementary five-site gaps. White diamonds mark means. The reflection about zero follows from the purity identity, numerically checked against directly calculated complementary scores.

Switching from three-site access to complementary five-site access reverses the gap while keeping the same encoding. This exact consequence of purity differs from the three reversals above, where removing disentanglers changed the encoding at fixed three-site access. For five-site access, the same MERA encodings favor uniform subsets, and the mean MERA-versus-tree acquisition changes become positive. A statement about an encoding's access preference therefore needs its access budget and collection law.

What would a sufficient collection description contain?¶

We can now make the missing information precise. Let $w$ be a probability vector on the 56 triples, and let $h_S=e(S)$ contain this source's subset information values. Normalization and measured collection statistics form linear constraints $Aw=b$. The observer's score is $h^\mathsf{T}w$.

For normalization and individual efficiencies, the first row of $A$ is all ones. Each of its next eight rows indicates whether a particular site belongs to each triple. Because every column contains exactly three memberships, the eight membership rows sum to three times the normalization row. The matrix therefore has a redundant constraint. We determine its rank with singular values instead of trying to invert $AA^\mathsf{T}$.

The paper's proposition on the sufficiency of a collection description states that, when the feasible family contains a strictly positive distribution, the constraints determine $h^\mathsf{T}w$ exactly when $h$ lies in the row space of $A$. If $h=A^\mathsf{T}c$, the score is $c^\mathsf{T}b$ for every compatible law. Conversely, if $h$ has a component outside that row space, a null-space direction changes its score. A strictly positive feasible law allows small movements in both directions while keeping probabilities nonnegative, making that failure observable within the feasible family.

Here $Ad=0$ but $h^\mathsf{T}d=\Delta\ne0$. The uniform law has weight $1/56$ on every triple, supplying the strictly positive feasible distribution required by the criterion. Both collection protocols satisfy every recorded constraint, yet they supply different amounts of diary information. The missing information concerns which sites arrive together. The row-space criterion tells us when additional collection measurements are sufficient to determine the score.

Which additional joint statistics would determine the desired score? A measured coincidence such as the frequency with which two specified sites arrive together adds a row to $A$. For a proposed set of measurements, one can ask whether the enlarged row space contains $h$. The notebook establishes the present insufficiency; selecting a minimal calibration set would require a separately specified optimization and measurement model.

From available information to retained possession¶

The controlled contrast has a direct place in the paper's physical argument. Information may be preserved in an encoding while the observer's description of collection leaves its available amount undetermined. Joint access must be evaluated against the correlations carrying the diary. The MERA study makes that dependence visible even after collection size and every individual efficiency have been fixed.

Receiving dynamics come next. In a separately supplied uniform flagged capture channel, let $p$ be the capture probability, $X$ the collected register, and $M$ the receiving memory. With no early side register, retained normalized reference information obeys $r=p e$. With an already held register $E$, the corresponding construction gives

$$I(Q:EM)=I(Q:E)+p\,I(Q:X\mid E).$$

The uniform flagged-transfer conditions are essential: the failure branch leaves an erasure flag, and the success branch transfers the complete collected register. These identities belong to the paper's receiving channel for an imperfect collected register. The present MERA calculation supplies access states and scores; it does not execute that receiver composition.

The manuscript also constructs a finite-switch, lossy two-site receiver for the HP inputs and an exact storage-noise ordering reversal for a five-carrier code. These are separate from the MERA comparison: the storage-noise example changes the receiving channel at fixed encoding, whereas the MERA/tree intervention changes the encoding at fixed collection laws. Neither receiving calculation is executed here.

A further MERA experiment would feed the collected MERA states into a finite receiver with an explicit capture channel. Holding the encoding, collection laws, and receiver resource and time budgets fixed would let us compare $I(Q:M)$, or $I(Q:EM)$ with side information, at a common deadline. It would require an explicit capture channel and its finite-error calculation. Additional joint-access calibration is another focused extension: hold the source and feasible collection family fixed, add measured joint-collection statistics, and calculate whether the enlarged constraints determine the target score. Larger networks, bond dimensions, or Hamiltonian-selected tensors would change the encoding study itself and need their own sampling plan.

How to check the results¶

In either mode, the notebook checks file identities, constructs the first MERA/tree pair from its tensors, recomputes encoding summaries and bootstrap distributions, and verifies collection and complementary-access identities. It also executes 66 causal-cone contraction checks and all three exact-null controls on the separate frozen pair. Regeneration mode additionally generates and compares the full ensemble.

The comparator requires exact inventories, shapes, data types, identifiers, seeds, scientific counts, and labels. Numerical validation uses $10^{-10}$: Frobenius norms for matrices, Euclidean norms for states, and absolute differences for scalars. The $10^{-8}$ threshold classifies resolved signs. Every run must satisfy its own tensor and checkpoint hashes, and nonfinite values fail validation.

Raw-negative-eigenvalue counts are checked within each run. Each state key must match one saved eigenvalue array; every value must be finite and at least $-10^{-10}$. Per-state negative counts and their aggregate must match those eigenvalues exactly. Recorded minima must agree within tolerance. Counts can differ between otherwise consistent runs when numerical rounding changes the sign of eigenvalues near zero.

For these random, unoptimized finite encodings, the observer's joint collection pattern changes available diary information even when individual efficiencies and collection size agree. The paired intervention separates the change in protocol preference from changes in acquisition itself. Access depends on both the encoding and which sites arrive together.
